content: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE) infections primarily occur in healthcare settings, such as hospitals. These infections can be prevented through proper infection control measures, and they are treatable with antibiotics other than vancomycin. Enterococci are bacteria that are naturally present in the human intestines, the female genital tract, and the environment, including soil and water. VRE refers to strains of enterococci that have developed resistance to vancomycin, a commonly used antibiotic for treating enterococcal infections. Most VRE infections are associated with hospital settings. In 2017, VRE was responsible for an estimated 54,500 infections among hospitalized patients in the United States, leading to approximately 5,400 deaths. Certain groups of people are at higher risk of developing VRE infections. These include individuals who have been on antibiotics, particularly vancomycin, for extended periods; those who have undergone surgery; individuals with medical devices such as catheters implanted in their bodies; and hospital patients, especially those with compromised immune systems. VRE spreads primarily through contact with contaminated surfaces or medical equipment, as well as through person-to-person contact, often via the hands of healthcare workers or caregivers. It is important to note that VRE does not spread through the air via coughing or sneezing. To reduce the risk of VRE transmission, patients and caregivers should practice good hand hygiene by washing their hands with soap and water or using alcohol-based hand sanitizers. Hand hygiene is particularly important before and after caring for wounds, touching medical devices, using the bathroom, or preparing food. Gloves should be worn when there is a possibility of contact with body fluids, such as stool or wound bandages. Patients or caregivers should inform healthcare providers if they or someone they care for has VRE. In healthcare settings, it is essential to allow staff to clean patient rooms daily to minimize the risk of contamination. Healthcare providers must adhere to strict infection control protocols to prevent the spread of VRE to other patients. Treatment for VRE infections involves the use of antibiotics other than vancomycin. To determine the most effective antibiotic, healthcare providers will collect a specimen from the patient and send it to a laboratory for testing. In some cases, individuals may carry VRE without showing signs of infection, a condition known as colonization. Colonization does not require antibiotic treatment. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is actively working to address VRE infections. This includes tracking VRE cases through the National Healthcare Safety Network and providing data through the Antibiotic Resistance (AR) & Patient Safety Portal. The CDC collaborates with health departments, federal agencies, healthcare providers, and patients to prevent VRE infections and slow the spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Additional resources, such as laboratory tools and antimicrobial susceptibility testing data, are available to support healthcare professionals in managing VRE infections.
